grounded_explanation_text: Top consideration is Melanoma (MEL), based on features (regular uniform features) observed in the photo [source: Bolognia JL, Schaffer JV, Cerroni L. Dermatology, 4th Ed, Ch. 113 (Elsevier, 2018)]. Also consider Other Benign Lesions and Benign Keratosis (Seborrheic Keratosis) as potential differentials because shared dermoscopic features can overlap [source: Soyer HP et al. Three-point checklist of dermoscopy. Dermatology 2004; 208(1):27-31]. On skin tone group G2, note that In darker skin types (Fitzpatrick IV-VI / Tone Group G3), melanoma disproportionately arises on non-sun-exposed acral sites including the soles of the feet, palms, and subungual nail beds (Acral Lentiginous Melanoma / ALM). Dermoscopically, ALM exhibits a diagnostic parallel ridge pattern (melanin bands along cutaneous dermatoglyphic ridges rather than furrows). Amelanotic or hypopigmented variants are frequently misdiagnosed as chronic ulcers, verrucae, or foreign body granulomas. [source: Bradford PT et al. Acral lentiginous melanoma: incidence and survival patterns in the United States. Arch Dermatol 2009; 145(4):427-434]. Recommended next step: Suspected melanoma requires immediate urgent specialist referral to a dermatologist or surgical oncologist. The standard diagnostic procedure is a complete narrow-margin (1-3 mm) excisional biopsy down to the subcutaneous fat. Partial shave or punch biopsy should be avoided if total excision is clinically feasible to ensure accurate Breslow depth staging. [source: NCCN Guidelines for Melanoma: Cutaneous, Version 2.2024].
